1:
A new voice enters the debate, and the witnesses mark at once how differently it opens: Elihu turns from the three friends to Job himself, and — alone among all the speakers — addresses him by name, "Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speeches." The reformed John Gill notes that in the foregoing chapter Elihu had bent his discourse chiefly against the three friends, blaming them, and here turns to Job, entreating his attention in a humble, suppliant manner; the very "wherefore" looks back to that reproof, for Elihu took not the part of the three, and, being full of matter and uneasy until he had vented it, he begs a diligent and attentive hearing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the several arguments by which Elihu presses Job not only to hear him patiently but to believe he designed him a good office and to take it kindly. Let Job consider, Henry says, that Elihu does not join with his three friends against him — he has disliked their proceedings, disclaimed their hypothesis, and set aside their method — so that Job should hearken to "all his words, and not to some of them only," for we cannot judge of a discourse unless we take it entire. And Elihu intended to make a solemn business of it, not to put in a word by the by nor give a short repartee to show his wit, but, after long silence, to speak with deliberation and design.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke stands back to survey the whole speech Elihu is opening, and lays out its plan: Elihu offers himself in God's stead to reason with Job in meekness and sincerity, charges him with irreverent expressions, and then vindicates the providence of God, showing the various methods he uses to bring sinners home — by dreams and visions, by secret inspirations, by afflictions, by messengers of righteousness, and by the great atonement. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the address a profession of integrity: Elihu begins by professing his sincerity, and, with reference to Job's own longing for an umpire in ch. 9:33 and one who would maintain his right with God in ch. 16:21, declares himself ready to be that man — one who, being like Job "made out of the clay," is disposed to deal favourably with him. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the stage for a mediator's speech, a younger man who claims neither the terrors of God nor the prejudice of the friends, but only a fair and attentive ear.
2:
Having begged a hearing, Elihu draws attention to the very act of his speaking: "Behold, now I have opened my mouth, my tongue speaketh in my palate." The reformed John Gill reads it as the overflow of a man too full to be silent — begun to speak in order to give vent to the fulness of matter within him, which made him, like bottles of new wine, ready to burst; and since he had opened his lips that he might speak and be refreshed, he sets somewhat before Job to induce him to listen. The gesture is not vanity, Gill implies, but the pressure of conviction seeking its outlet.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the connective and the ceremony of the line. The word that stands at the head of this new turn is the verumtamen used elsewhere in the book, as in ch. 13:4, subjecting the whole discussion to the one condition that Job listen not to this or that but to its entire connected contents. And Elihu, they observe, addresses Job by name, as none of the previous speakers had done; with the "behold now" of ch. 13:18 he directs Job's observation to what he is about to say — a circumstantial statement, that he has already opened his mouth, his tongue is already in motion, which solemnly inaugurates what follows with a consciousness of its importance. The very phrase "my tongue speaketh in my palate," they note, belongs to that solemnity, the organs of speech named one by one to mark the deliberation of a man who has weighed his words before uttering them. Where Job had felt the absence of "words of uprightness" (ch. 6:25) in the speeches of the three, Elihu can at the outset ensure that his own word will be such.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the same gesture the mark of a man who intends no light or hasty thing. After long silence Elihu opened his mouth with deliberation and design; upon mature consideration he had already begun, and was prepared to go on if Job would encourage him by his attention. It is the manner, Henry implies, of one who weighs his matter before he utters it. The witnesses converge less on any dispute within the verse than on its tone: this is the formal, weighed opening of a speech its author believes worth the hearing, and the very solemnity of the announcement — the opened mouth, the moving tongue — is itself a kind of pledge that what comes will be considered, deliberate, and sincere.
3:
Elihu pledges the temper of all he is about to say: his words shall be "of the uprightness of my heart." The reformed John Gill is careful that Elihu does not make his own integrity the subject of his discourse, but its spring: what he speaks will proceed out of the uprightness of his heart, in all sincerity and faithfulness, the real sentiments of his mind, and not the product of a double or insincere heart. The wesleyan-arminian voices press the source and the clearness of it. Adam Clarke grounds it in the Spirit named in the next verse — "as God has given me his Spirit, from that Spirit alone will I speak" — so that all his words shall be of uprightness, and "knowledge clearly," which he renders "pure science": he will lay down no false position and draw no false consequence. John Wesley keeps it plain and pastoral: "I will not speak passionately or partially, but from a sincere desire to do thee good," and what he speaks will be plain, not hard to be understood.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the honesty this claims, and turns it into a quiet reproof of the three friends. Elihu resolves to speak as he thought and not otherwise: his words shall be the genuine product of his convictions and sentiments. There was reason to suspect, Henry says, that Job's three friends did not think, in their consciences, that Job was so bad a man as they had represented him to be merely for the support of their hypothesis; and that was not fair. It is a base thing to condemn with our tongues, to serve a turn, those whom at the same time we cannot but think well of in our hearts; Elihu is an honest man and scorns to do so.

Henry draws from it the general rule that those who speak of the things of God should carefully avoid all obscurity, both of notion and of expression, and speak as plainly and clearly as they can; for by that it appears that they themselves understand what they speak of, that they mean honestly, and design the edification of those they speak to. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the verse a double pledge — sincerity of heart and clearness of speech — by which Elihu deliberately sets his coming argument apart from the passionate and partial pleading Job had suffered from his three comforters, promising a word that is at once honest in its motive and lucid in its delivery.
4:
"The Spirit of God hath made me" — and Elihu grounds both his competence and his humility in the single fact of his creation. The reformed John Gill takes the words first as a plain confession that every man is made by God and not by himself, and then as a proof of the deity of the Spirit, who was concerned not only in garnishing the heavens and moving upon the face of the waters but in the very formation of man; Father, Son, and Spirit are the Makers of man, spoken of in the plural. The wesleyan-arminian voices hear an unmistakable echo of the creation narrative. Adam Clarke marks the plain allusion to Gen. 2:7, the words for "the breath of God" and "hath given me life" recalling how the Lord "breathed into his nostrils the breath of lives, and man became a living soul." John Wesley draws the practical point Elihu means by it: "I am thy fellow creature, and am ready to discourse with thee upon even terms, according to thy desire."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers these threads into Elihu's argument for a hearing. He owns himself unfit to enter the lists with his seniors, yet begs they will not despise his youth, for he is God's workmanship as well as they, made by the same hand, endued with the same noble powers and faculties, and designed for the same great end; and therefore why may not the God that made him make use of him as an instrument of good to Job? Henry turns it, as is his manner, into a summons to every reader: God has made us and given us life, and therefore we should study to use our life to some good purpose, spending it in glorifying God and serving our generation according to his will, that we may answer the end of our creation, and it may not be said that we were made in vain.

The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as at once Elihu's credential and his modesty. The same breath of the Almighty that formed him fits him to speak — for the rational soul he received is from the Spirit of God — and yet that same creation levels him with the man he addresses, so that Job need fear no unequal contest. What in one clause is a warrant for the young man's boldness is in the next a pledge of his gentleness, both drawn from the one truth that he too is a creature of God's making.
5:
Elihu now throws the debate open, inviting Job to reply if he can: "If thou canst answer me, set thy words in order before me, stand up." The reformed John Gill reads it as an offer of full and fair liberty: when Elihu had done speaking, and Job had heard him out, if he thought he could make a reply he was welcome to it — a request that tacitly asks of Job the same attentive and candid hearing Elihu had begged, and promises the same in return. It is the challenge of a man confident of his ground, yet willing to be answered.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of the turn that runs on to the great charge, rendering the sequence plainly: "set thy words in order before me, stand up. Behold, I am according to thy wish in God's stead: I also am formed out of the clay. Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee." The invitation to "stand up" is the summons of a court, where a defendant is bidden rise and marshal his plea; and the whole of it, they note, leads to the undeniable fact Elihu is about to establish, that Job has said in his hearing things which cannot be left unanswered.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the offer both fairness and self-restraint. Elihu was very willing to hear what Job could object against what he had to say: "If thou hast so much strength and spirit left thee, and art not quite spent with the distemper and the dispute, set thy words in order, and they shall have their due consideration." Those that can speak reason, Henry observes, will hear reason; a man sure of his cause does not dread a reply but courts it. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Elihu, unlike the friends who had pronounced and re-pronounced their verdict, opens his case as a debate rather than a sentence — bidding Job rise, order his words, and answer if he is able, and offering, in the verses just ahead, the very equality of standing that will make such an answer possible. The confidence is real, but it is the confidence of one who invites examination rather than one who forecloses it, and it prepares the ground for the gentleness he is about to promise.
6:
"Behold, I am according to thy wish in God's stead" — and here Elihu names the office he has come to fill, the very daysman Job had cried out for. The reformed John Gill takes it in two ways at once: Elihu undertakes to be an advocate for God, vindicating his justice in his dealings with men and with Job, and beseeching him, as in God's stead, to submit patiently to his providence and wait the issue; or else, reading the Hebrew as "I am as thou art," Elihu presents himself as one who belongs to God, a sinful, frail, mortal creature like Job, accountable as he is, and just such a one as Job had wished for to dispute the point with him. The wesleyan-arminian voices lean to the second sense. Adam Clarke follows Mr. Good's rendering, "Behold, I am thy fellow; I too was formed by God out of the clay," taking the disputed word not as "according to thy mouth," that is, thy wish, but as a term signifying fellow, equal, or like. John Wesley holds both together: "I will plead with thee in God's name and stead, which thou hast often wished, and I am God's creature like thyself."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on how exactly Elihu answers Job's own longing. How pathetically had Job wished, "O that one might plead for a man with God!" and "O that I knew where I might find him!" — only stipulating that God's dread should not make him afraid, as in ch. 13:21. "Now," says Elihu in Henry's paraphrase, "look upon me, for this once, as in God's stead: I will undertake to plead his cause with thee, and show thee wherein thou hast affronted him; and what appeals or complaints thou hast to make, make them to me." And Henry seizes on the second clause as the ground of comfort: "I also am formed out of the clay" — Elihu, like the first man of Gen. 2:7, and like Job who had pleaded "thou hast made me as the clay" in ch. 10:9, is of the same mould. It is good, Henry adds, that those who are to us in God's stead are so, that he speaks to us by men like ourselves. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the meeting of Job's wish and Elihu's offer — a mediator of clay, standing in God's place yet on Job's level.
7:
The promise of a mediator of clay is now made explicit as a promise of gentleness: "Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee." The reformed John Gill sets the verse against Job's own longing for a contest he need not dread. Job had wished that God's fear might not terrify him nor his dread make him afraid, that so he might freely reason; and now, Gill says, Job has nothing to fear from Elihu, who is a man and not God, with no terrible majesty about him — no clod of the same clay could inject the dread that the appearance of the divine Majesty would. Elihu, Gill adds, was no great personage, neither king nor prince, nor in any civil authority, nor had he so much as age to command an awe, much less to strike dread and terror; Job might therefore reason with him freely, on equal ground. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke ties the words directly to Job's plea in ch. 9:34, "Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me": being Job's equal, Elihu can impose no fear that would overawe him and unfit him to conduct his own defence. "We are on equal terms," Clarke has him say; "now prepare to defend thyself."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses the second clause with a single stroke — "neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee," that is, "I will deal gently with thee, and not be harsh." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the principle the verse embodies. Elihu would not assault Job with the terror his friends had used, nor draw up the heavy charge against him that they had, nor overwhelm him as the appearance of God would; standing on the same level and made of the same mould, he could not, and would not, impose that terror. And Henry lifts it into a rule for all who would do good by reproof: "If we would rightly convince men, it must be by reason, not by terror; by fair argument, not by a heavy hand." Job had desired a judge to decide his appeal, and Elihu is one according to his wish, a man like himself. The witnesses do not divide; they hear in the verse the whole method Elihu proposes — persuasion without dread, argument without weight of majesty — the gentleness of a mediator who knows that a man crushed by fear cannot plead, and who therefore lays his terror aside before he begins.
8:
The preface ended, Elihu comes to his charge, and grounds it not on rumour but on his own ears: "Surely thou hast spoken in mine hearing, and I have heard the voice of thy words." The reformed John Gill notes that Elihu took up the accusation neither on suspicion nor on report nor on the word of others, but on what he had heard himself, unless he were greatly mistaken, which he thought he was not. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the point that Elihu was an ear-witness of what he reproves: Job had said it in his hearing and in the hearing of all the company, not in private conversation, but openly, and therefore it was fit he should be openly reproved for it. Those that sin before all, Henry adds, must be rebuked before all; and when we hear anything said that tends to God's dishonour, we are concerned to bear our testimony against it, for "ye are my witnesses, saith the Lord," to confront the accuser. What is said amiss in our hearing we are bound to reprove, and Elihu does but discharge that duty openly which had been openly incurred.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the charge honest by observing that what Elihu says here, and in the three verses following, is in the main simple quotation from Job's own words, or their obvious sense, as the reader may see by turning to ch. 13:27, ch. 14:16, and ch. 31:4. Henry is fairer still, and notes where Elihu may press too hard: Job had not said in so many words that he was clean without transgression — nay, he had owned himself impure before God — but he had said "thou knowest that I am not wicked" and "my righteousness I hold fast," on which Elihu might ground the charge. It was true, Henry grants, that Job was a perfect and upright man, and not such a one as his friends had made him; yet he ought not to have insisted so much upon it as if God had wronged him in afflicting him. Those who speak passionately and unwarily, Henry cautions, must thank themselves if they are misunderstood. The witnesses do not divide over the fact that Job had spoken amiss; they only weigh, with Henry, how far Elihu's summary of Job's words is exact and how far it sharpens them, agreeing that what is said to God's dishonour, once heard, ought to be answered.
9:
"I am clean without transgression, I am innocent; neither is there iniquity in me" — Elihu puts into Job's mouth the plea of a spotless man, and the witnesses divide over how fairly the words are fastened on him. The reformed John Gill grants that no man is naturally clean or free from sin, that man came clean from the hands of God but by sin is become unclean, and that Job himself clearly held this; yet since Elihu so peremptorily affirms the words were spoken in his hearing, Gill inclines to think they did drop from Job's lips in the controversy, though not recorded, for not everything said on both sides is preserved, only so much as the Holy Ghost thought fit. No man is naturally clean, Gill adds, nor clean by any doing of his own, whether by moral actions, ceremonial washings, or even his own tears and humiliation; and of this Job was clearly and fully sensible. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott flatly denies that Job ever used this language; but many of his statements were capable of being so perverted, as in ch. 16:17 and ch. 27:5. This shows, Ellicott says, that even Elihu was incapable of entering fully into Job's position: he did not understand that a man can be righteous only in proportion as he trusts God, and, trusting, is righteous with God's righteousness — the very truth Job was faintly but surely striving after.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley threads the needle between the two. Job meant "clean," not absolutely, for he often confessed himself a sinner, but as one guilty of no such transgression as might give God just occasion to punish him so severely; and thus far, Wesley says, Elihu's charge was just, and herein it differed from the charge of the three friends. They accused Job of hypocrisy for asserting his innocence; Elihu accuses him on other and truer grounds, because Job's justification of himself was accompanied with reflections upon God. The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, gives the plain rendering and the tension it holds: knowing himself righteous, and still treated as an enemy, Job had cried out against a God who "findeth occasions" against him — and it is that outcry, not the bare claim of integrity, that Elihu means to answer. The witnesses do not finally divide over Job's real state; they divide over the report of his words, Ellicott charging Elihu with misconstruing a man he could not comprehend, Wesley crediting him with a sharper and juster aim than the friends had, and Gill supposing the words were truly, if unrecordedly, said.
10:
The charge sharpens as Elihu quotes what he takes to be Job's complaint against God's very method: "Behold, he findeth occasions against me, he counteth me for his enemy." The reformed John Gill unfolds the sting in "findeth" — as though God sought in order to find, inquired after Job's sins and searched diligently that he might have something to bring against him; and, not finding great enormities, sought after lesser ones, and, failing there, went back as far as the sins of his youth, all to pick a quarrel. Mr. Broughton, Gill notes, renders it "lo, he picketh quarrels against me," and others read the word as "staggerings" or "totterings," the frailties and infirmities of a man. But this, Gill insists, is precisely the misrepresentation Elihu means to correct: it would be needless for God to seek in order to find occasions against men, since there is enough ready at hand; and to represent the Lord as dealing thus with a good man is to wrong him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that Elihu is here reporting Job's own earlier words, pointing back to ch. 13:24, ch. 13:26, and ch. 19:11, where Job had complained that God hid his face and held him for an enemy. The verse thus stands as a faithful, if unflattering, echo: Elihu is not inventing a grievance but gathering up the accusations Job had scattered through the debate, that God watched over his sin, counted him a foe, and treated the sufferer as a criminal to be hunted.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, in reproving the same words, brings out what makes them a fault. To say that God "findeth occasions" supposes that he seeks them, as an enemy seeks a pretext; and Job had spoken to this purport, "Dost thou not watch over my sin? He counteth me for his enemy." Henry does not deny Job's affliction, but the construction Job had put on it — that a God who is good and just should hunt a man's faults and set himself against him as a foe. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse is Job's real language, honestly reported, and that its error lies not in feeling the weight of the affliction but in reading into it a divine malice, as though the Almighty were a suspicious adversary raking up old faults to justify a quarrel he had already resolved upon.
11:
Elihu completes his quotation of Job with the image of a prisoner shackled and watched: "He putteth my feet in the stocks, he marketh all my paths." The reformed John Gill hears in it more than the pain and disgrace of affliction. The stocks are the punishment of offenders, a security against escape and a reservation for further punishment; and by using the figure Job had suggested not only that his afflictions were painful and inescapable, close-fettered as they were, but that they were inflicted as punishments, so that he was handled as a criminal, a malefactor guilty of some notorious breach of the law. It is that construction, once more, that Elihu will answer — the reading of chastisement as though it were the sentence of a condemned man.

The wesleyan-arminian and grammatical-historical voices trace the words to their source in Job's earlier speech. Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott alike refer the line back to ch. 13:27, where Job had first said that God set his feet in the stocks and looked narrowly to all his paths; Elihu is quoting, not caricaturing. John Wesley glosses the last clause with the suspicion Job had felt in it: God "narrowly prys into all my actions, that he may find matter against me" — the vigilance of a jailer or a prosecutor rather than the care of a father. Gill adds that Job took his afflictions not merely as painful and disgraceful, and such as he could not extricate himself from, close-fettered as he was, but as inflicted upon him for punishment, so that he was dealt with as a criminal who had committed some notorious breach of the law.

The witnesses do not divide over the meaning of the figure, and their very agreement measures the gravity of what Elihu is charging. Job's complaint, gathered here into one vivid picture, is that the God who afflicts him has made himself a warder: the feet fast in the wooden clamp so that the sufferer can neither flee nor stir, every footprint noted and kept in evidence, the whole life dogged and hemmed in as a felon's is. That the words are Job's own, and painfully sincere, none of the witnesses doubts; but the burden of the coming argument is that a good man in the dark may thus mistake the hand that holds him, reading confinement where there is discipline, and surveillance where there is love, and calling that a prison which was meant, as the next verses will urge, to keep his soul back from the pit.
12:
Having gathered Job's complaints, Elihu delivers his verdict on them: "Behold, in this thou art not just: I will answer thee, that God is greater than man." The reformed John Gill is careful how narrowly the censure runs. Elihu does not deny that Job was a just man, before God in an evangelical sense and before men in a moral one; he detracts nothing from Job's general character as one who lived soberly, righteously, and godly. But in this — in insisting so much on his own innocence, and tacking to it such unbecoming reflections on God's dealings — he was not just, for he did not give God his due nor represent him rightly. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke puts the point sharply: Job had laid charges against God's dealings but had not been able to justify them, and, were there nothing else against him, these irreverent speeches are proof enough that he is not clear in the sight of God. John Wesley expands the "greater": God is greater than man not only in power and majesty but in justice, wisdom, and goodness, and therefore Job does foolishly to censure his judgments, casting off the awe and reverence he owes his sovereign Lord.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott raises a candid question against Elihu's fairness: had not Job said the very same thing? For in ch. 9:2 and following Job had confessed that a man cannot be just with God — and is it possible to think otherwise, Ellicott asks, especially as Elihu here uses the word that specially means man in his frailty? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks how much gentler Elihu's charge is than the friends': they would not own Job just at all, but Elihu says only, "in this thou art not just." Many that are just yet in some instance do not speak like themselves; we must neither flatter a good man in his errors nor draw his whole character from a few misplaced words, for "in many things we all offend." And Henry finds in Elihu's one plain truth an argument to silence all complaint: God is greater than man — greater not merely in strength, so that it is vain to contend, but in holiness, justice, and goodness, so that it is absurd to find fault. The witnesses do not divide over the substance; they weigh only whether Elihu, in convicting Job of injustice toward God, has himself dealt justly with a man who had confessed as much before him.
13:
Elihu presses his charge with a question that exposes the presumption in Job's complaint: "Why dost thou strive against him? for he giveth not account of any of his matters." The reformed John Gill hears the absurdity in it — a creature striving against his Creator, the clay against the potter — and reckons it weakness and folly in Job to wish to litigate the point with God, and sin to chide with him or complain of any of his dealings; for men cannot answer him one of a thousand, as Job himself had owned. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the second clause into the ground of a quiet submission: is it not useless to contend with God, and can he do anything that is not right? As to giving thee a reason why he deals thus, thou needest not expect it; he is sovereign, and not to be summoned to the bar of his creatures. It is enough, Clarke says, to know that "he is too wise to err, and too good to be unkind." John Wesley reads the reticence the same way: God uses not to give his creatures an account of the grounds of his judgments, being the supreme governor in whose will it becomes all men to acquiesce.

Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott enters a pointed defence of Job, and the reading here genuinely divides. Job, Ellicott insists, had not striven against God; he had only expressed his longing to come into judgment with him, as in ch. 23:3. Job was striving with and against the darkness that lay round about God's throne, not against the justice of God, which he entirely trusted; so that Elihu, in framing the question as he does, has again mistaken the man. Ellicott notes too the alternative rendering of the last clause, "for none can answer any of his words," though he judges the received version preferable. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry stands with the plainer sense: those who complain of God strive against him, implead and impeach him; and it is unreasonable for weak, foolish, sinful creatures to strive with a God of infinite wisdom, power, and goodness, who is under no obligation to show us a reason for what he does. The witnesses divide, then, not over God's freedom from account — all grant it — but over Job himself: whether he had truly striven against God, as Elihu, Gill, Clarke, and Henry take it, or had only wrestled, trusting, with the mystery about God's throne, as Ellicott contends.
14:
"For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not" — and with this Elihu turns from rebuke to his real doctrine, that the God who "giveth not account" nevertheless speaks, again and again, to save. But the witnesses divide over what the "once, yea twice" means. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley hear a promise of repeated admonition: God speaks once in dreams and visions, and a second time by chastisements, or, more simply, speaks over and over, giving line upon line, so that when one warning is neglected he gives another, not willing that any should perish. Wesley reads it so: when once speaking does not awaken men, God is graciously pleased to give them another admonition. On this reading the numeral marks God's patience, his willingness to try method after method.

The grammatical-historical voices, with Adam Clarke, hear rather an enumeration of distinct modes. Keil and Delitzsch take the verse to open the description of the first mode in which God speaks — himself coming forward as a witness in man's sleep, by dreams and dream-like visions — and note that the detailing of the night-vision in the next verse is formed after the pattern of ch. 4:13. Clarke says the general statement is now to be unfolded in the six methods gathered from the verses that follow, and Ellicott lists the two ways to be dilated on through the rest of the chapter, instancing Abimelech in Gen. 20:3 and Nebuchadnezzar in Dan. 4:5 as examples of this first, nocturnal method.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a meditation on the two parties to the verse — God's friendship to our welfare and our enmity to it. It is a token of his favour, Henry says, that despite the distance sin has made he is pleased to speak to us at all, and to speak of our own concerns, telling us our faults and warning us of our danger; and this he does "once, yea, twice," that is, again and again, so that sinners may be left inexcusable. Yet man perceives it not — heeds it not, discerns it not, stops his ear, and rejects the counsel of God against himself. Henry sets the frame for all that follows: God speaks by conscience, by providences, and by ministers, and even now, when he seemed to Job to keep him in the dark and treat him as a stranger, he was telling him his mind and doing him a kindness. The witnesses do not divide over that gracious purpose; they divide only over the numeral — whether "once, yea twice" measures the repetition of God's patience or enumerates the several channels through which he speaks.
15:
"In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed" — Elihu names the first way God speaks, and the witnesses attend both to the mode and to its defence. The reformed John Gill notes that this was God's most usual way in those times: sometimes he spoke to a prophet in public office, that he might deliver it to others, and sometimes directly to persons themselves, as to Abimelech and to Laban. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix a small textual point that guards the sense: the better reading and the accentuation keep "vision of the night" and "dream" as two notions, not one, and the whole detailing of the scene is modelled on the night-vision of Eliphaz described earlier in the book. It is in this condition of deep or half sleep, when the bodily senses are locked up, that God prepares the ear for a confidential communication.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke divides the verse into its two clauses and mounts a defence of both against the scoffer. The dream comes "when deep sleep falleth upon men"; the vision, "in slumberings upon the bed," when a man is between sleeping and waking, or lies awake in the dark wrapped in deep contemplation, the night having shut out all objects so that the mind is not diverted by images of earthly things. Many salutary warnings, Clarke urges, have come this way, and to decry them all because there are many vain dreams would be as wise as to deny the Bible because there are many foolish books; the impression they made and the good they wrought were the proofs of their divine origin. Of one such vision, he adds, the book itself gives a remarkable account in ch. 4:12 and following, which seems to have fallen upon Eliphaz in the night season.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the season its spiritual fitness. It is a good time for men to retire into their own hearts and commune with them when they are upon their beds, solitary and still; and this is the time God takes for dealing personally with men. When he sent angels on his errands he commonly chose that hour, when by deep sleep the senses were sealed and the mind more free to receive the immediate communications of divine light. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the stillness of the night, far from being empty, is one of God's chosen rooms for speaking, and that the dream and the vision are not superstition but a real, if now less common, channel of his warning voice.
16:
What the night-vision accomplishes is told next — "Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction" — and over that sealing the witnesses genuinely divide. The reformed John Gill takes the opened ears to be the internal ears: while the bodily ears remain shut in sleep, God opens the heart or understanding to attend to and receive the things delivered in the vision. Keil and Delitzsch, a grammatical-historical voice, render the phrase of a confidential preparing of the ear by the removal of hindrances, so that God "openeth the ear of men, and sealeth their admonition" — the warning stamped, as with a seal, upon the mind. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke heads this the method of secret inspirations, and insists that a dream simply considered does no good; it is the opening of the understanding and the pouring in of the light that make men wise to salvation — the serious alarms, holy purposes, and penitential pangs by which the divine Spirit withdraws men from evil. John Wesley keeps it briefest: "sealeth — he imprints those instructions upon their minds."

Against this settled reading the other grammatical-historical witness turns the sense the other way. Charles Ellicott, comparing "my transgression is sealed up in a bag" in ch. 14:17, takes the sealing not of instruction received but of chastisement decreed: God opens their ear to show that he will decree, confirm, and seal up the sentence to be executed upon them if they will not repent; and only if the word be taken in the sense of instruction must it mean that he will complete and confirm it. So the verse yields two readings — a seal set upon the admonition to fix it in the heart, or a seal set upon the threatened judgment to ratify it against the impenitent.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the gentler sense at length. God gives the admonition admission and makes it heeded: he opens the ear that was stopped, works in the soul a submission to conscience, as when he says in Isa. 50:5, "God hath opened my ear, and I was not rebellious." Then he gives it lodgment, sealing the instruction that is designed for them, making the soul receive its deep and lasting impression as wax takes the seal; when the heart is delivered into the divine instruction as into a mould, the work is done. The witnesses do not divide over God's aim — to fasten his word within — but over the thing sealed, most reading it of the saving admonition, Ellicott alone of the sentence that hangs over the man who will not hear.
17:
The purpose of that sealed instruction is now declared: "That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man." The reformed John Gill glosses "his purpose" as his wicked work, whether one begun or one designed — as Abimelech was restrained by a dream from taking Abraham's wife, and Laban from harming Jacob; God speaks in the night to turn a man back from the very sin he had set his hand to. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes this the main point of Elihu's whole teaching: rather, "that he may withdraw man from carrying out his evil actions, and may remove that pride from man which he secretly cherishes." The purposes of God, on Ellicott's reading, are disciplinary, meant to keep man from the sin he would otherwise be prone to commit; and in just this way Job might have been a righteous man and yet be justly chastened, lest he should prove unrighteous — a preservative, not a punishment.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fastens on how the hiding of pride is wrought. By these glorious representations of his divine majesty to man, God takes him off from the admiration of his own excellency, brings him to a sight of his own weakness, and so to a humble and ready submission to his will; the pride is "hidden" because its object, a man's fancied worth, is eclipsed by the vision of God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws both clauses together. To withdraw man from his purpose is to change the temper of his mind and the course of his life, to make him leave off the world's work and the flesh's and set him to the work of God; many a man has been stopped in the full career of a sinful pursuit by the seasonable checks of his own conscience, saying, "Do not this abominable thing which the Lord hates." And God does this especially by hiding pride from man — hiding from him the things that feed his pride, taking his mind off them, setting before him reason to be humble; or, as some read it, taking away pride from man, plucking up that root of bitterness. All whom God has mercy in store for, Henry says, he will humble and hide pride from, for pride makes men eager and resolute in their sinful purposes, and so he withdraws them from those purposes by mortifying their pride. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the whole design of the night-warning is moral and merciful — to break off a sin before it is done, and to lay low the pride that would drive a man on to do it.
18:
The rescue that all this aims at is stated plainly: God does it "that he may keep back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword." The reformed John Gill reads the pit in a double depth — the pit of the grave, where the body corrupts and turns to dust, and the bottomless pit of everlasting ruin; and he sets the verse in the frame of a Father's discipline, that the Lord's people are reproved by him that they may not be condemned with the world. The saving warning of conscience, on Gill's reading, stands between a man and both deaths, the temporal and the eternal. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the plainer, outward sense and marvels at it: by taking such warnings how many have been snatched from an untimely end — some prevented from perishing by the pit, some sudden accident, and others delivered from the sword of the assassin or the nocturnal murderer. Examples in every kind, Clarke says, could easily be given, but the reader's own knowledge may spare the commentator the trouble. John Wesley keeps it short and inward: God does it "by his gracious admonitions, whereby he leads him to repentance."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his running theme of the mercy hidden in restraint. While sinners are pursuing their evil purposes and indulging their pride, their souls are hastening apace to the pit, to the sword, to destruction, both in this world and in that to come; but when God, by the admonitions of conscience, withdraws them from sin, he thereby keeps back their souls from the pit and saves them from perishing by the sword of divine vengeance, so that iniquity shall not be their ruin. That which turns men from sin, Henry says, saves them from hell; it saves a soul from death, as James 5:20 declares. And he draws the tender moral: see what a mercy it is to be under the restraints of an awakened conscience, for faithful are the wounds and kind are the bonds of that friend, since by them the soul is kept from perishing eternally. The witnesses do not divide; whether they weigh the outward deliverance from a violent death, as Clarke does, or the inward rescue of the soul from hell, as Gill, Wesley, and Henry do, they agree that the whole severe machinery of dream, opened ear, and mortified pride has this one gracious end — to hold a man back from the brink he could not see.
19:
Elihu passes to a second and severer lesson: "He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones with strong pain." The reformed John Gill marks the "also" as introducing a new way in which God speaks — by afflictions, and sometimes painful ones, which have a voice in them that men of wisdom will hear; and this is not the pain of a wounded spirit but of the body, felt on the very bed where a man looks for ease and rest. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke heads it the method of affliction, and recalls how such chastening was the cause of David's recovery, who could say, "Before I was afflicted, I went astray," in Ps. 119:67. Clarke lingers, with his usual curiosity, over "the multitude of his bones," reading it of diseases, especially the rheumatic, in which every bone seems broken or out of joint; and he cannot forbear to number them, counting the bones of the human frame to above two hundred, every one of which may become a seat of pain upon the sufferer's bed.

The grammatical-historical voices refine the wording. Keil and Delitzsch note the disputed phrase — whether the man is chastened "he and the vigorous number of his limbs," so that his once-strong frame is now the theatre of pain, or whether it is "the unceasing conflict of his limbs" that torments him. Charles Ellicott offers the same alternative, rendering it "with continual strife in his bones," and instances rheumatism and gout; this, he says, is the second manner in which God speaks, first by dreams and now by sickness. John Wesley marks it simply as "the second way whereby God instructs men and excites them to repentance."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry describes the patient in his extremity with a physician's eye and a preacher's heart. Pain and sickness turn a bed of down into a bed of thorns, on which he that used to sleep now tosses to and fro till the dawning of the day; the case as here put is very bad, for it is not the smarting of the flesh that is complained of but the aching of the bones, an inward, rooted pain, and not one bone but the multitude of them. See, Henry says, what frail, what vile bodies we have, which, though receiving no outward hurt, may be thus pained from causes within themselves; pain is the fruit of sin, yet by the grace of God the pain of the body is often made a means of good to the soul. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that God's second voice is louder and more grievous than his first, that the sickbed is a pulpit, and that the very bones may be made to preach repentance to a man who slept through the gentler warning of the night.
20:
The sickness deepens until the body turns against its own nourishment: "his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat." The reformed John Gill reads the common but telling symptom — through the force of pain the sufferer loses all appetite, and even a nausea takes hold, so that he loathes as the most abominable thing even bread, which is so necessary to human life, so strengthening to the heart, and never wearisome in health; it stands here for all common and useful food, now become hateful to him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confirms the observation from the sickroom: these expressions strongly and naturally point out that general nausea, or loathing, which the sick feel in almost every kind of disorder, when the very sight of food is unwelcome.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording that carries the picture forward. The contracted future form is poetic, and the sense runs on into the next verse — his flesh vanishes "from sight," so that it is seen no longer, or "from comeliness," so that it becomes unsightly; the second, they note, comparing the language of 1 Sam. 16:12 with Isa. 53:2, might be preferred. The failing appetite and the wasting flesh are, in their reading, one continuous movement of decay, the loathing of food being the visible beginning of the ruin that will strip the body to the bone.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the same clause, turns it to a lesson on the vanity of the appetite men so pamper. His life abhorreth bread, the most necessary food, and dainty meat, which he most delighted in and once relished with pleasure — a good reason, Henry says, why we should not be over-desirous of dainties, since they are deceitful meat, as Prov. 23:3 warns; we may be as soon made sick of them as we are now fond of them, and those who live in luxury when they are well may, by reason of sickness, come to loathe the very dainties they doted on, and so, with grief and shame, read their sin in their punishment. The time may come, he adds from Ps. 107:18, when a man shall loathe the sight of meat and draw near to the gates of death. The witnesses do not divide; they read the lost appetite as one of God's plainest sermons in the flesh — that the body which had been the servant of pleasure is now unable to receive even its necessary bread, and that the whole of a man's dainty living is exposed, on a bed of sickness, as a deceitful and fleeting thing.
21:
The wasting runs its course, and the sufferer is reduced to a skeleton: "His flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen; and his bones that were not seen stick out." The reformed John Gill reads the double ruin of it — the flesh all gone, none left to be seen, nothing but skin and bones, and this partly through the vehemence of strong pain and partly through the loathing of food; unable to take anything for the nourishment and support of the fluids, the body is quite emaciated. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke names the diseases that leave a man so, glossing the verse of atrophy, marasmus, and consumptive complaints in general, in which the flesh melts from the frame and the bones that were buried in it start into view.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch work at the finer grain of the Hebrew. The flesh vanishes, they render, so that it becomes unsightly; and in the second clause the received text and the marginal reading differ, whether we read the noun "and a wasting" or the verb "and they are wasted away," from a root meaning to grind, gnaw, or rub away — the very bones, as it were, ground down and worn thin. The radical notion, they say, is that of a rubbing away, a slow attrition of the body under the file of disease; and the once-hidden bones, laid bare, are the visible measure of how far the attrition has gone.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the ruin against the strange endurance of the soul. By sickness, perhaps a few days' sickness, the flesh that was fat and fair is consumed away till it cannot be seen; it is strangely wasted and gone, and the bones, which were buried in flesh, now stick out, so that you may count his ribs and tell all his bones. Yet the soul that is well nourished with the bread of life, Henry adds, sickness will not make lean, though it soon makes so great a change in the body. The witnesses do not divide; they gather around one grim tableau — the wasted flesh, the protruding bones, the man melted almost to nothing — and read it as God's severest bodily sermon, the frame that seemed so strong reduced in a few days to a rack of bones, that a proud creature might learn, in his own dwindling body, how frail a thing he is and how near the grave he stands.
22:
The wasting brings the man to the very edge of death: "Yea, his soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers." The reformed John Gill is careful with the words. The soul, strictly speaking, is not laid in the grave, but returns to God who gave it; here "soul" stands rather for the body, or for the person of the sick man, whose disease is so threatening that all hope is gone, and he is given up by physicians and friends, seemingly at the grave's mouth — the very apprehension, Gill notes, that Job had of himself earlier in the book. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the deepening of the case. This second lesson, they observe, is the harder, which the Greek version rightly distinguishes from the first; for it treats now not merely of a warning against sin, but of a deliverance from the death to which sin has almost abandoned the man — and such a deliverance, as the next verse will show, requires a mediator. The course of the thought, they add, will not let us take that mediator for a mere human messenger.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the two nouns. Here "soul" is the immortal spirit, distinguished from the animal life named in the parallel clause; the one draws near to the pit, to corruption, the other to "the destroyers," which Mr. Good would render "the Destinies," supposing the Hebrew to name what the Greeks meant by their Fates and the later peoples by the angel of death. Clarke himself thinks the plainer sense the more natural, taking the destroyers of the pangs of death that are ready to seize a dying man. John Wesley agrees, glossing the destroyers as "the pangs of death, here called the destroyers," which are just ready to lay hold of him.

The witnesses do not divide; they hold the verse at the hinge of the whole discourse. All that has gone before — the night-vision, the opened ear, the sickbed, the wasting flesh — has brought the man down to this point, his soul at the grave's brink, his life in the grip of the destroyers. And it is precisely here, in the extremity where warning can do no more and the sufferer lies all but abandoned, that Elihu's argument turns from the diagnosis of God's severity to the announcement of his rescue. The darkness is at its deepest just before the messenger and the ransom are named, and the witnesses feel the pause: this is the last verse of the descent, the ground from which grace will lift a man who has nothing left in himself to plead.
23:
"If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness" — and here the witnesses divide most sharply of all, over who this messenger is. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great takes him for Christ himself: who is this Angel, he asks, but the one the prophet calls the Angel of mighty counsel in Isa. 9:6? For to declare good tidings is to "evangelize," and so the Lord, announcing himself to us, is called an Angel; and well does the text say a messenger speaking for man, since, as the apostle says in Rom. 8:26, he intercedes for us — the great Physician who heals his patients, sometimes by like and sometimes by contrary remedies. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the interpreter, one among a thousand, as a remarkable anticipation of that office of Advocate with the Father discharged in 1 John 2:1 and Heb. 7:25: it is impossible, he says, for those who hold all Scripture inspired not to see here an indication of what God would afterwards teach of the mediation of the Son and the intercession of the Spirit; and he renders the clause "to declare concerning that man his uprightness," to plead his cause and be his advocate.

The reformed John Gill will not have the messenger a created angel, though angels do attend the dying; rather a minister of the word is designed, who is by office an angel, a messenger of Christ and an interpreter of the Scriptures, and such a faithful evangelical minister is scarce and rare, one among a thousand, whose business is to visit the sick and show them the uprightness and faithfulness of God in afflicting them. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads him more plainly still as "a prophet or teacher," to expound the providence and point out God's design, a person rightly qualified for so great and hard a work, of whom there are but very few. Adam Clarke takes him for a mediatorial or interpreting angel or messenger, "one from the Chief, Head, or Teacher," sent to declare to man his righteousness. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the human minister — a man of wisdom who knows the voice of the rod and its interpretation, one of a thousand, whose advice and help are as needful in sickness as a good physician's. So the debate stands unresolved: is the interpreter Christ himself, or an anticipation of his advocacy, or a mediating angel, or simply a faithful minister sent to read the meaning of the affliction? The witnesses agree only that his errand is grace — to show a suffering man his uprightness and turn him toward mercy.
24:
The messenger's plea is heard, and grace breaks in: "Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the last clause as the heart of the gospel hidden in Job. When God finds a gracious heart he will be found a gracious God, and here he gives both a gracious order for the sick man's discharge — "let him be delivered" — and a gracious reason for it: "I have found a ransom." That ransom, Henry says, is Jesus Christ, so Elihu calls him, as Job had called him his Redeemer; for he is both the purchaser and the price, the priest and the sacrifice, so high was the value put upon souls that nothing less would redeem them, and so great the injury of sin that nothing less would atone for it than the blood of the Son of God. It is a ransom of God's own finding, the hidden wisdom no man or angel could have devised, and God glories in the invention — "I have found it; I, even I, am he that hath done it."

The wesleyan-arminian voices read it the same way. Adam Clarke heads this the method of atonement, taking the word for a propitiation, and finds the redemption of a lost world not obscurely signified here, God so loving the world, as in John 3:16, that he gave his Son that whoever believes might not perish; it is this atonement that gives efficacy to all the preceding means. John Wesley hears God himself speaking: "Although I might justly destroy him, yet I will spare him, for I have found out a way of ransoming sinners from death, which is the death of my Son, the Redeemer of the world."

The reformed John Gill takes the ransom for Christ, on the foot of whose redemption God the Father is gracious to the sick man for his Son's sake. The grammatical-historical witnesses are more restrained but converge. Keil and Delitzsch place the ransom in the flow of a real deliverance from death, which the mediator's intervention has procured; and Charles Ellicott stresses what the verse itself insists — it is God who finds the ransom, as it was by God's grace the interpreting angel was forthcoming, so that it is not man's righteousness that saves him but the ransom God has provided, even where God justly recognises what righteousness there was in the man. These words, Ellicott adds, must have fallen on Job's ear with a grateful sound, confirming his longing for the daysman of ch. 9:33. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether they name the ransom outright as Christ's atonement or hold to its place in the story, all agree that the deliverance is God's free gift, found and provided by him, and received by a man who could not ransom himself.
25:
The ransom accepted, the wasted body is renewed: "His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth." But the witnesses divide over whether the freshness is of the body or the soul. The reformed John Gill reads a literal recovery from sickness through the gracious dealing of God — not that the flesh becomes absolutely as a child's, but comparatively: he who was reduced to skin and bone is now fat and plump, his dried and withered flesh moist and juicy again, his wrinkled skin soft and smooth, his pale face grown ruddy. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep to the same restored body, noting how the tense changes as the flesh "swelleth with the freshness of youth" and the man returns to his younger days, and weighing the older versions that read the verse of flesh once weakened or wasted now made whole.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the clause the other way, to a spiritual renewal. His flesh fresher than a child's means he shall be born a new creature; his return to the days of his youth, that he shall be born again and become a child of God through faith in Christ Jesus. On Clarke's reading the recovery Elihu describes is not merely of health but of the whole man, made young in the second birth. So the reading genuinely divides: whether the promise is of a sick man risen from his bed, or of a sinner risen to newness of life.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, who allows that bodily recovery does not always follow repentance but sometimes does, holds the two together in the order of the gospel. When the patient becomes a penitent, a blessed change follows: interest him in the ransom, and then his flesh shall be fresher than a child's, and he shall return to the beauty and strength of his youth. Recovery from sickness, Henry says, is a mercy indeed when it arises from the remission of sin, for it is then, as Isa. 38:17 has it, in love to the soul that the body is delivered from the pit of corruption, God casting our sins behind his back; and so the Saviour said first, "thy sins be forgiven thee," and then, "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk," in Matt. 9:2. The witnesses do not finally divide over the mercy; they weigh only how far the renewed flesh is a healed body and how far a regenerate soul, agreeing that the youth restored here is the visible token of a deeper deliverance already wrought within.
26:
The recovered man turns to prayer and communion: "He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him; and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness." The reformed John Gill takes the verse of the frame of the soul after the body's healing, the spiritual blessings that follow: whether the prayer that first brought recovery, or, as the connection rather suggests, the thanksgiving of the man restored, who entreats the Lord to make him thankful and to show that his affliction was sanctified, leaving him more holy and more humble than before. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the spirit of prayer as the very breath of the new life: being adopted into the heavenly family, the man now has it; God manifests his good will, and he sees God's face with joy — with exultation — for, being justified by faith, he has peace with God and rejoices in the hope of glory. And "he will render unto man his righteousness" Clarke takes of grace enabling the convert to live to God's glory and then rewarding the work as if it were his own. John Wesley glosses "render" briefly: God will deal with him as with one reconciled through the mediator, and turning from sin to righteousness.

The grammatical-historical voices keep the same picture and ground it in the faith of the fathers. Keil and Delitzsch render the sequence — he prays, God shows him favour, he beholds God's face with joy, and thus God recompenses to man his uprightness — and carry it on into the confession of the verses that follow. Charles Ellicott calls it a very beautiful description of the penitent's restoration: he shall thankfully resort to the house of God with joy, for that God has rewarded him according to his righteousness, which was itself the fruit of faith, as in Gen. 15:6 and Ps. 32:1.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the whole recovery of peace. The patient, being a penitent, has learned to pray, and prays for pardon and for health; his prayers are accepted, God's anger is turned away, and the light of his countenance shines on the soul. Then follows the comfort of communion — "he shall see the face of God, which before was hid from him, and see it with joy," as Jacob said, "as though I had seen the face of God," in Gen. 33:10 — and a blessed tranquillity of mind arising from the sense of justification, God rendering to this man his righteousness, that he may receive the atonement, as Rom. 5:11 speaks. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the healed body is only the outward sign of a soul restored to prayer, to favour, to the sight of God's face, and to the peace of a righteousness reckoned to it by grace.
27:
The restored man breaks into open confession, and the witnesses work at both the grammar and its sense: "He looketh upon men, and if any say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not." The reformed John Gill lays out the two ways the opening may be taken. On the received version God looks upon men, observing all their ways, and particularly regarding the afflicted, that when they are penitent and confess he may restore them; but most, Gill says, carry it the other way, of the recovered man himself, who looks upon his friends and relations about him, or goes among them, or ranges them in order that he may address them, or, as some render it, sings before them in a joyful and exulting strain the confession that follows. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott prefers this latter reading, rendering it "He looketh upon men, and saith, I have sinned" — that is, this is the confession of the restored sinner — though he notes the alternative "he shall sing before men," which he thinks hardly so probable.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole of God's shining into fallen man and the answer it draws out. God shines into wretched, fallen men to convince them of sin; and if any, under that convincing light, says, "I have sinned, and perverted the right" — abused the powers and mercies God gave him, seeking rest in the creature — "and it profited me not," rendering the last clause "it was not equal to me," it did not come up to my expectation nor supply my wants, being all vanity and vexation of spirit. The confession, on Clarke's reading, is the cry of a man who has tried sin and found it empty.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out what the words teach of sin and of repentance. Here is the nature of sin — the perverting of that which is right, a most unreasonable thing, the rebellion of the creature against the Creator, the perverting of the right ways of the Lord, as Acts 13:10 speaks, so that the ways of sin are called crooked ways in Ps. 125:5. And here is what is to be got by it — "it profited me not"; the works of darkness are unfruitful, and all the gains of sin come far short of its damage, as the penitent owns in Rom. 6:21. True repentance, Henry says, confesses the fact of sin — "I have sinned" — the fault of it — "I have perverted that which was right" — and the folly of it — "it profited me not." The witnesses divide only over the speaker of the confession, whether God is said to look for it or the healed man to sing it out before others; they agree that the words are the genuine language of a broken and returning heart.
28:
"He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light" — the confession closes on rescue and light, though the witnesses part over whose voice speaks and how the verbs run. The reformed John Gill reads it plainly of the deliverance promised: God will keep the man's soul from the pit of the grave, and, more, from the pit of hell or perdition. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens it to the whole penitent world: God will do for every individual returning sinner what he has promised in his word for a lost race, delivering his soul from going down to the pit of hell, so that his life shall see the light, walking in the light as Christ is in the light, and enjoying a clear sense of acceptance through the blood of the Lamb. John Wesley reads both a temporal and an eternal deliverance — his endangered life restored and continued, and, yet further, his soul delivered from going into the pit of hell, his life seeing the light, all good, in the vision and fruition of God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a textual point that turns the verse into the sufferer's own words. There are two readings in the Hebrew, one of which the received version follows; but the better, Ellicott judges, is "He hath redeemed my soul from going into the pit, and my life shall see the light" — this being part of the restored man's confession, continued from the verse before, until the speaker resumes his own reflection in the summary that follows. So the difference is real: whether the line is Elihu's statement in the third person, that God will deliver such a man, or the penitent's grateful testimony in the first, that God has redeemed his soul and his life shall see the light.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the promise into the general rule Elihu is drawing. If any man humble himself with such a confession, whoever he be, he shall not come into condemnation but be saved from the wrath to come; God shall deliver his soul from going into the pit, so that iniquity shall not be his ruin, and he shall be happy in everlasting life and joy, his life seeing the light, that is, all good, in the vision and fruition of God. To obtain this, Henry adds, if the prophet had bidden us do some great thing would we not have done it? how much more when he only says, confess and be pardoned, repent and be saved. The witnesses do not divide over the rescue; they weigh only whether it is announced of the penitent or confessed by him, and agree that the end of the whole discipline is a soul lifted from the pit into the light of the living.
29:
Elihu now sums his doctrine: "Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man." The reformed John Gill reads it as a recapitulation of all that has gone before — God is an operating Being, always at work in providence, sometimes on the mind in dreams and visions, sometimes by affliction, sometimes by his messengers and ministers of the word, and all according to the inward actings of his own eternal purpose. And these he works "oftentimes," or, as the Hebrew has it, "twice": when once is not sufficient he repeats it, warning by one dream and then another, sending one affliction and then another, and continuing the ministry of the word, waiting to be gracious until all his ends are answered with the man who is the darling of his care. The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the same numeral. Adam Clarke renders the word "twice three times," or, as the dual and the following term suggest, "three times over" — again and again, very frequently — God using one method or another, or all of them, to bring even the stout-hearted, far from righteousness, home to holiness and heaven. John Wesley keeps it briefest: "all these ways God uses to convince and save sinners."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the great and gracious design that binds the whole together. All these things God is working with the children of men: he deals with them by conscience, by providences, by ministers, by mercies, by afflictions; he makes them sick and makes them well again, setting the one over against the other, as Eccl. 7:14 teaches, yet with his hand in all. All providences, Henry says, are to be looked upon as God's workings with man, his strivings with him; he uses a variety of methods to do men good, and if one affliction do not the work he will try another, and if neither, he will try a mercy, and will send a messenger to interpret both. He often works such things twice, thrice — a plain echo, Henry notes, of the "once, yea twice" with which the passage opened — changing his method and returning to it, that a soul may by some means be reached. The witnesses do not divide; they gather the chapter into one confession, that the God who seemed to Job an enemy is in truth a patient and untiring worker for man's welfare, repeating and varying his approaches, and refusing, so long as there is hope, to give a soul up to the pit.
30:
The end of all God's dealings is named at last: "To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living." The reformed John Gill reads the pit in more than one depth — the grave, on whose brink the sick man had lain, from which God turns him back by restoring his health, as in Hezekiah's case; and, figuratively, the pit of an unregenerate state, a corrupt and comfortless grave in which men lie dead in trespasses, from which, in conversion, souls are brought back and quickened. The grammatical-historical voices ground the phrase in Scripture and doctrine. Keil and Delitzsch render it of bringing back the soul from the pit that it may be enlightened with the light of life; and Charles Ellicott calls this the very key-note of Elihu's teaching, that God's dealings are for the purpose of education and discipline. Adam Clarke hears an echo, indeed a quotation, of Ps. 56:13 — "thou hast delivered my soul from death, that I may walk before God in the light of the living."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets this end beside the earlier one to show the sweep of God's mercy. The former method, by dream and vision, was to "keep back" the soul from the pit, to prevent the sin before it was committed; this later one, by sickness and the word, is to "bring back" the soul, to recover those who have fallen in, that they may not lie still and perish. If God did not take more care of us than we do of ourselves, Henry says, we should be miserable; we would destroy ourselves, but he would have us saved, and devises means, by his grace, to undo that by which we were undoing ourselves — and all that they may be enlightened with the light of the living, having present comfort and everlasting happiness.

Here, though, the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley turns and disputes the Calvinist edge of Henry's comfort. Granting the gracious design that God would save men from being for ever miserable, Wesley presses the objection against the doctrine that so much done to save the lost renders those who perish inexcusable: "But how much did God do to save them? Did he ever do anything to save them? Did he ever design to save them? If not, how does that which was never done, nor designed, render them inexcusable?" It is a genuine clash of schools over the reach of God's saving intent. The witnesses agree on the goal — a soul brought back into the light of life — but part over its extent, Henry finding all the reprobate left without excuse, and Wesley protesting that no man can be inexcusable for slighting a salvation never meant for him.
31:
His argument summed, Elihu turns back to Job with a fresh plea for attention: "Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak." The reformed John Gill glosses it simply — consider and weigh well what has been said, or rather attend to what is yet to be said, and be silent while it is delivered. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives it the same weight in fewer words: pay the deepest attention to what I have said and to what I shall say. The verse is a hinge, gathering up the doctrine just laid down and asking of Job the very silence and heed with which a learner receives instruction; it is not the silence of a man overborne, but the stillness in which alone a weighty matter can be taken in.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the appeal forward as one connected movement, rendering the three verses together — "Listen, O Job, hearken to me; be silent and let me speak on. Yet if thou hast words, answer me; speak, for I desire thy justification. If not, hearken thou to me; be silent and I will teach thee wisdom." On their reading the "mark well" of this verse is not a bare command but the opening of a courteous exchange, in which Elihu will both offer Job the floor and, if Job has nothing to say, resume his own teaching.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in it Elihu bespeaking Job's acceptance of all he had offered, and begging him to mark it well, for what is intended for our good challenges our regard. It is the request of a teacher who does not wish to overbear his hearer but to be genuinely weighed; and Henry reads the whole close of the speech as governed by that spirit — Elihu will neither run Job down with words nor demand a silence that is mere submission, but asks the attentive stillness in which alone instruction can be received. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse marks the turn from argument to application, Elihu pausing to secure Job's ear before he presses his lesson home, and asking of him not defeat but attention — the silence not of a man overpowered but of one willing to learn. What is offered for a man's good, the witnesses imply with Henry, has a just claim upon his serious and undivided regard.
32:
Elihu tempers his call for silence with a generous offer of reply: "If thou hast anything to say, answer me: speak, for I desire to justify thee." The reformed John Gill takes it plainly — if Job has anything to object to what has been delivered, or any answer to return to the charge laid against him, let him speak. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it the fairness of a man who wants his opponent cleared: "If thou hast any thing to say, now answer, now speak freely; for it is my desire that thou shouldst stand clear of all charges." The invitation is not a formality; Elihu genuinely holds the floor open, wishing Job not silenced but vindicated.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the sense of that desire to justify. Elihu wishes to justify Job before his friends — to maintain that his afflictions are not on account of past sin, but as a preservative against a possible future defection; and this being so, he considers that Job's case may justly be defended and Job himself vindicated against the three. It is the whole difference between Elihu and the friends, gathered into a clause: they came to condemn, and he to acquit, if only Job will let his complaints against God be corrected.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on this generosity as the mark of a true reprover. If Job has anything to say for himself, in his own vindication, let him answer; "though I am fresh, and thou art spent, I will not run thee down with words." Elihu contends for truth, Henry observes, not, as the friends did, for victory; and those we reprove we should desire to justify, and be glad to see them clear themselves from the imputations they lie under, giving them all possible advantage and encouragement to do so. It is a rare temper in a disputant — to press a charge home and yet to long for the accused to be proved right — and Henry marks it as the difference between one who seeks to win an argument and one who seeks to do a man good. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Elihu's demand for silence is no tyranny, since it is joined to a standing offer of reply and a sincere wish to see Job justified, so that the whole exchange is conducted as a search for truth in which the reprover would rather lose his point than see his hearer wronged.
33:
The speech ends as it began, with a plea to hear: "If not, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom." The reformed John Gill glosses it briefly — if Job has no objection to make nor answer to return, let him attend and listen to what Elihu has further to lay before him. The chapter closes, that is, on the same note of attentive silence with which it opened, the offer of reply having been made and, in the event, declined; for Job says nothing, and none of the three friends chooses to intermeddle further.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, taking his leave of the chapter, adds a rich concluding note on both text and sense. He records the various readings that the manuscripts and versions carry in the closing verses — "his righteousness" or "according to his righteousness," "his soul" or "my soul," "his life" or "my life," "shall see the light" or "shall be as the light" — by which the confession of the restored man may be read in the first person throughout, as a penitent's own prayer and testimony. And Clarke offers a paraphrase that reads the whole passage of Christ: the Messenger who prays unto God and makes intercession for transgressors, being the Mediator between God and man; the Father who is favourable and restores to wretched man his righteousness, creating the soul anew through the great atonement named in v.24; and the penitent who cries, "Redeem my soul from going down to destruction, and my life shall see the light." This, Clarke concludes, is one of the best, the deepest, the most spiritual, and most important chapters the reader has yet met with in the book of Job — a grand exhibition of the way of salvation as revealed to patriarchs and prophets.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the plain lesson of the last verse. If Job has nothing to say against what has been offered, Elihu lets him know he has more to say, which he desires him patiently to attend: "Hold thy peace, and I will teach thee wisdom." Those who would both show wisdom and learn it, Henry says, must hearken and keep silence, be swift to hear and slow to speak; Job was wise and good, yet even such may be wiser and better, and must set themselves to improve by the means of wisdom and grace. The witnesses do not divide; they close the chapter where it opened, on the summons to a teachable silence — Elihu still pressing his suit, still offering to instruct, and still asking of Job only the quiet, attentive ear in which wisdom can be received.
